883.title: George Herbert
883.hook: a country parson poet: Love bade me welcome, yet my soul drew back
883.howItsDone: Herbert's poems are read in Anglican and other churches, and several have become hymns; the Church of England remembers him each year with a commemoration in its calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the King James Bible, built on Tyndale's work and made for the ear. Your line was the language of heaven, in english.

A guest stands at an open door. The host says come in, you're welcome. And the guest hangs back on the step. Muddy shoes. Empty hands. Not sure about a place at this table. That stubborn hanging back is the whole subject of a short poem by an English country parson. It begins: "Love bade me welcome: yet my soul drew back". The parson, the story goes, was a gifted man who could have had a career at court, and chose a small parish instead, writing poems that, tradition says, he wasn't even sure anyone should read.

George Herbert was a priest in the Church of England. His poems were gathered in a book called The Temple, published after his death. The story goes that he sent the manuscript to a friend, asking him to publish it if it might help some troubled soul, and to burn it if not. The friend published it. The last poem in one part of the book is called Love, and it's a conversation at a door. Love invites the speaker in. The speaker draws back, guilty of dust and sin. Love, quick-eyed, comes closer, asking gently if anything is lacking. A guest worthy to be here, the speaker answers. Love says: you will be. I'm unkind and ungrateful, the speaker objects, I can't even look at you. Love takes his hand and smiles: who made the eyes but I? One last way out: if he can't be a guest, he'll work, and serve the meal. And Love says no: sit down, and taste my meat. The poem ends with six plain words: "So I did sit and eat." No speech, no grand conversion. Just a person who stops arguing and accepts the seat. Some readers hear the Lord's Supper in it, Holy Communion. Others hear the banquet of heaven, or simply the shape of grace. Either way, it can be harder to be welcomed than to be useful, and Herbert lets Love win the argument by being kind.

If you can, find Herbert's Love, the third poem of that name, and read it slowly; if not, hold its first line and its last: love bade me welcome; so I did sit and eat. Then sit, and notice where you hang back from being welcomed: by a person, by rest, by God if you believe in God. If you pray, simply accept the seat; if you don't, practice sitting without earning it.
George Herbert. An English country parson whose poem Love tells of a soul that draws back from welcome, argues, tries to serve instead, and finally sits down and eats.
Your line: love bade me welcome. The seat was never something to earn. Until tomorrow.

884.title: John Donne
884.hook: a poet-dean: no man is an island; any man's death diminishes me
884.howItsDone: Donne's words are read at funerals and memorial services, and in some parishes a bell is still tolled for the dead, with prayers for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, George Herbert, and a soul that finally sat down to eat. Your line was love bade me welcome.

A man lies sick in bed in London, too ill to get up. Through the window comes a church bell, tolling slowly, the way a passing bell rang when someone in the parish was dying. He doesn't know who it's for. Instead of finding out, he turns the thought over, and writes. That sick man had once written daring love poems, then became a priest and the dean of St Paul's Cathedral in London. Out of that sickbed came a few lines that still turn up far from any church.

John Donne wrote his Devotions during a serious illness: meditations, prayers and arguments with himself about sickness, death and God. In one, he hears the bell and wonders whether it's tolling for someone he doesn't know, or, if he's sicker than he thinks, for himself. Then comes this, in modern spelling: "No man is an island, entire of itself; every man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main". The main is the mainland. A little later: "any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind". And he ends: "never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee." Donne uses man the way his century did, for every human being, which is why today's line says no one. His point is sharper than a pleasant feeling of connection. In his view, a stranger's death actually takes something from each of us, because we're part of the same body of humankind. Some readers hear Paul behind it. Paul describes the church as one body with many parts, in the King James Bible: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." Donne stretched that body wide. Every bell, every funeral, every name in the news is, in his picture, a clod of earth washed away by the sea.

Start with something close, the chair under you, your clothes, the last thing you ate, and ask quietly: who grew it, sewed it, drove it here? Let the faces you'll never meet come to mind, and follow one thread back to the field, the factory, the ship, feeling yourself a piece of the continent. If you pray, hold them all before God for a moment; if you don't, rest in being part of the main.
John Donne. A poet who became a priest and dean of St Paul's, who wrote from a sickbed that no one is an island, and that the tolling bell tolls for each of us.
Your line: no one is an island. The bell is never only for a stranger. Day eight hundred eighty-four.

885.title: The Pilgrims and the Puritans
885.hook: crossing the Atlantic for religious freedom; their story with Native peoples is honestly mixed
885.howItsDone: Congregational and other churches in New England trace their roots to the Pilgrims and Puritans, and some now hold services of remembrance and reconciliation with Wampanoag and other Native communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Donne and a bell heard from a sickbed. Your line was no one is an island.

A small, crowded ship called the Mayflower drops anchor off a cold coast in late autumn. At the heart of the group on board are English Christians who wanted to worship their own way, without the Church of England telling them how. Many have already lived as exiles in Holland. Others on the ship came for land and work. The version told in school pageants ends with a shared harvest feast. The real story is longer and harder, and it belongs just as much to the people already standing on that shore.

First, two names that get mixed up. The Pilgrims were Separatists: they believed the Church of England was beyond fixing, so they left it. The Puritans, who came after them and settled around Boston, wanted to stay in the church and purify it from within. Both crossed the Atlantic for the freedom to worship as they believed God wanted. The Puritans' leader John Winthrop told his settlers they would be like a city upon a hill, with every eye on them. He was reaching for Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." Now the people on the shore. The land around Plymouth was home to the Wampanoag. The Pilgrims' own governor, William Bradford, wrote that after a hard first winter, an English-speaking Native man named Squanto came to help, showing them how to plant corn and where to fish, and that a peace was agreed with the Wampanoag leader Massasoit. Bradford also wrote that Squanto had learned English after being carried off from his home. That peace held for a time. Later generations broke it, in land taken and in war. And the Puritans who came for freedom punished or banished some who worshipped differently, as tomorrow's story shows. So the story is honestly mixed: real faith, real courage, real help received, and real harm done. Which is why today's line is a question.

Wherever you're sitting, people lived on this ground before the town around you had its name. Feel the floor, and the earth beneath it, and bring to mind the people who walked here first, whose names you may not know yet. If you pray, remember them before God; if you don't, hold them in respectful attention.
Mayflower. The ship that carried the Pilgrims across the Atlantic to a shore already home to the Wampanoag, in a story of real help and real harm.
Your line: freedom for whom? A question worth keeping open. Day eight hundred eighty-five, done.

886.title: Roger Williams
886.hook: banished from Massachusetts, he founds Rhode Island with freedom of conscience for all
886.howItsDone: Baptists and others in America honor Roger Williams as an early champion of religious liberty, and his idea of soul liberty is still taught in churches that hold to freedom of conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mayflower, the Pilgrims and the Puritans: real help and real harm. Your line was freedom for whom?

The court in Massachusetts has decided: the young minister must leave the colony. His crime isn't theft or violence. It's ideas. He's been saying that the government has no business punishing people for how they worship, and that the king's charter can't hand over land that belongs to the Native peoples who live on it. Tradition says he slipped away in winter, before they could ship him back to England, that Native people sheltered him, and that Narragansett leaders let him settle on their land. There he founded a settlement where nobody would be punished for their conscience. He called it Providence.

Roger Williams was a Puritan himself, and an intense one. He wasn't arguing that faith didn't matter. He was arguing that it mattered too much to be forced. A belief pressed on someone at the point of a sword, in his view, isn't faith at all. He leaned on a parable of Jesus. A farmer sows good seed, and an enemy comes by night and sows weeds among the wheat. The servants want to pull the weeds out at once. The farmer says no, in the King James Bible: "lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest". For Williams, that settled it. Sorting true believers from false isn't a job for magistrates and courts. It's God's, at the harvest. This freedom came to be called soul liberty: the freedom of each person's conscience before God, which no government should touch. He pictured a hedge or wall between the garden of the church and the wilderness of the world, to protect the garden. And he lived it. His colony became a place where Baptists, Quakers and Jews could worship openly. He disagreed sharply with some of them in public debates, but he didn't drive them out. He learned the Narragansett language, wrote a book about it, and insisted land be bought from its people rather than simply taken. He could be prickly and stubborn. But the idea he was banished for traveled a long way.

Put a belief you think is wrong into one sentence, the way someone who holds it would say it, fairly, with no sneer. Then say quietly: they have the right to believe this; not that they're right, but the choice is theirs. If you pray, rest with let both grow together until the harvest; if you don't, let the other person stand, unharvested, in your mind.
Roger Williams. A Puritan minister banished from Massachusetts, who founded Providence as a place where no one would be punished for their conscience, a freedom that came to be called soul liberty.
Your line: soul liberty. Faith that matters too much to be forced. That's day eight hundred eighty-six.

887.title: George Fox and the Quakers
887.hook: a shoemaker's apprentice hears there is one, even Christ Jesus, who can speak to your condition
887.howItsDone: In a traditional Quaker meeting for worship, Friends sit together in silence with no set sermon, and anyone who feels moved may stand and speak briefly before the silence returns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Roger Williams, banished into the winter for a free conscience. Your line was soul liberty.

A young man in England has been put to work with a shoemaker. Something inside him is restless, and he walks from minister to minister with his questions. In his journal he remembers one telling him, more or less, to take up tobacco and sing psalms. Another, he says, got angry when he stepped on the edge of a flower bed. Nobody can reach him. He wanders, fasts, walks alone in the fields with his Bible. His name is George Fox, and what happens next starts a movement that sits down together in silence.

Fox describes the moment plainly. When all his hopes in other people were gone, and nothing outside himself could help, he heard a voice that said, in his journal's words, "There is one, even Christ Jesus, that can speak to thy condition." And then: "my heart did leap for joy." The voice doesn't hand him a new argument or a better minister. It says someone can speak to his condition: not the human condition in general, but his own, the exact shape of his restlessness. Fox came to believe the light of Christ could reach any person directly, a shoemaker as much as a scholar, a woman as much as a man. The people who gathered around him called themselves Friends. Others called them Quakers, and the name stuck. In a traditional Quaker meeting, people sit together in silence, with no set sermon. If someone feels moved to speak, they stand and speak, briefly, and the quiet returns. The silence isn't empty. It's waiting. There's an old story behind that kind of waiting. The prophet Elijah stands on a mountain. A wind tears at the rocks, but God is not in the wind. Then an earthquake, then a fire, and God is not in them either. And after the fire, in the King James words, "a still small voice." Friends sit down expecting that voice could come to anyone in the room. Other Christians pray with set words, music and liturgy, and they too speak of God meeting them there.

Sit the way Friends sit, as if something might be said: not clearing your mind, not making anything happen, hands resting, letting the sounds in the room pass. If you pray, hold Fox's words loosely: someone can speak to my condition. If you don't, simply wait, and notice what rises in the quiet without chasing it.
Quakers. The name given to George Fox's Friends, who gathered to wait together in silence for the light of Christ to speak to each person directly.
Your line: speak to my condition. Yours, exactly as it is. Day eight hundred eighty-seven, done.

888.title: Bunyan in jail
888.hook: a tinker imprisoned for preaching dreams the story that becomes Pilgrim's Progress
888.howItsDone: Christians in different churches read The Pilgrim's Progress at home, aloud with children, or in study groups, following Christian's journey a few chapters at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, George Fox, the restless seeker, and the Quakers' waiting silence. Your line was speak to my condition.

John Bunyan mends pots and pans for a living. He's a tinker, with a tinker's hands and very little schooling. He also preaches, without a license from the Church of England, and in his England that's against the law. So he's put in the county jail in Bedford. He can go home, he's told, if he promises to stop preaching. He won't promise. The months in a cell turn into years, and his family outside struggles without him. A man with a hammer and no pulpit now has neither. What he does have is time, and a pen.

Listen to how the book he's remembered for begins: "As I walked through the wilderness of this world, I lighted on a certain place where was a Den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep: and, as I slept, I dreamed a dream." A den. Old editions carry a note in the margin saying what the den is: the gaol, the jail. From the first sentence, the book hints it was dreamed behind bars. The dream is The Pilgrim's Progress. A man named Christian carries a heavy burden and sets out from the City of Destruction toward the Celestial City. On the way he meets characters with names you can't forget: Evangelist, who points the way, Obstinate and Pliable, Mr. Worldly Wiseman, Faithful, Hopeful, Giant Despair in his castle. Bunyan writes plainly, and Bible phrases run all through his pages. Here's why the jail matters. Bunyan couldn't walk anywhere. So he wrote a book that is nothing but walking: roads, hills, sloughs, valleys, gates. The man who was stuck gave readers a journey. Long before him, the apostle Paul wrote letters from his chains. To the Philippians, from prison, Paul writes that what happened to him has "fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel." Bunyan seems to have believed something like that about his cell. The waiting wasn't wasted. It became the dream.

889.title: The burden rolls away
889.hook: in Bunyan's story, Christian's burden falls off at the cross and rolls into a tomb
889.howItsDone: Christians bring their burdens to God in different ways: in personal prayer, in confession or the sacrament of reconciliation, at the communion table, or by laying a written worry at the foot of a cross in some churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bunyan in jail, and Evangelist pointing the way. Your line was the dream in the jail.

A heavy backpack does something strange on a long hike. At first you feel every pound. Then you stop noticing, you lean forward without knowing it, and your shoulders forget what light felt like. Only when you set it down do you realize how bent you'd become. Bunyan's pilgrim starts like that. The first picture of him is a man in rags with a great burden on his back, reading a book and crying out, What shall I do? He carries that weight through the slough, past the gate, mile after mile. Today, in the story, it finally comes off.

Christian runs, with difficulty, up a road fenced with a wall on either side, to a place that rises a little. At the top stands a cross, and below it, a tomb. Here's how Bunyan tells it: "Just as Christian came up with the Cross, his burden loosed from off his shoulders, and fell from off his back, and began to tumble, and so continued to do, till it came to the mouth of the Sepulchre, where it fell in, and I saw it no more." Look at what Christian does in that sentence. Nothing. He doesn't untie the straps or throw it off. He arrives, and the burden loosens. Bunyan, a Protestant preacher, is picturing what he believed about grace: that what Christ did on the cross lifts a weight a person can't lift alone. The burden falls into the sepulchre, which some readers take as Christ's own tomb, and the narrator never sees it again. Christian stands looking at the cross, amazed, tears running down his cheeks. Then he says, "He hath given me rest by his sorrow, and life by his death." Rest. That reaches back to Jesus in Matthew's gospel: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." Christians from different churches describe how that rest comes in different ways: through baptism and the sacraments, through faith, through confession, through a lifetime of being made new. Bunyan's picture is one man's dream of it. And the road doesn't end at the cross. Christian keeps walking, lighter now, with a long way still to go.

Name one weight you've carried so long you've stopped noticing it: a grudge, a worry, a regret. Breathe out and let your shoulders drop, as if the straps had loosened on their own. If you pray, bring it to the cross, or rest with come unto me; if you don't, let it be set down for now.
Sepulchre. In Bunyan's dream, the tomb at the foot of the cross where Christian's burden tumbles in and is never seen again.
